On Wednesday Israeli security forces were reported to have withdrawn from the Jewish settler outpost in the village of Qusra near Nablus, following clashes with a crowd of extremist settlers. About a dozen settlers are said to remain at the site. After the Palestinian homeowners made their initial report to the Israeli army, the first soldiers who arrived at the scene were filmed praying with the settlers.
Israeli security forces have reportedly withdrawn and about a dozen settlers are said to remain at the site where two families have been besieged since Sunday.

The Abu Ridi and Hassan families have been posting on social media appealing for help after their water and power supplies were cut off and their food stocks ran low. It is not clear exactly what the settlers in Qusra want. In the past, settlers have forced Palestinians out of their homes and seized their properties. The stated aim of the settlers is to empty the area of its Palestinian residents. The latest developments come as a top UN official told the Security Council in New York on Tuesday that "the West Bank is at breaking point". All settlements are illegal under international law. Outposts are set up without official Israeli authorisation. Palestinian security camera footage shows settlers tearing down a wall outside the Abu Ridi family's home on Sunday evening and using the stones to block the road.

This left seven people - including two young girls – unable to leave their homes while other Palestinians could not reach them. They live in what is known as Area B, part of the West Bank under Palestinian administrative control and Israeli security control. Posting on Facebook, Qusay Abu Ridi said the situation was critical, "especially as we are completely isolated". He wrote: "We are living in our own home, on our own land, and we are asking for nothing more than the right to live safely and with dignity." Aysha Hassan told Reuters the settlers had "tried to break the gate" to the house and "started throwing stones at us, cursing and insulting us". She said her family was "dying of fear, extremely terrified".

He wrote: "We are living in our own home, on our own land, and we are asking for nothing more than the right to live safely and with dignity."

Aysha Hassan told Reuters the settlers had "tried to break the gate" to the house and "started throwing stones at us, cursing and insulting us".

She said her family was "dying of fear, extremely terrified".

On Monday, Israeli settlers blocked Israeli journalists from the left-leaning Haaretz newspaper from trying to reach the Palestinian properties. The reporters said Israeli soldiers at the scene refused to help them when their car was blocked for two hours. They were told the area was a closed military zone
